Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

the audio guide is available in english during the trial and visitors can ask the desk for a transcript if listening is not convenient the staff have a second set of instructions for school groups because teachers sometimes collect several handsets together and return them in one batch the group instructions ask the teacher to count the devices before leaving the desk and again at the end of the visit no deposit is required and the staff do not reserve handsets in advance on busy days the desk may ask a group to wait while returned devices are checked and charged the trial notes will continue to include equipment costs, charging problems, and comments about particular tracks", "output": "We installed the new audio guide at the north entrance on a Monday in April, after the old handsets began losing their charge before lunchtime. The museum kept the galleries open during the change, and visitors could still borrow a paper map while the staff tested the devices at the desk. Each handset has a small screen, a speaker, and one raised button for starting or pausing a track. The volume controls sit on the side, and the numbered track list appears after the welcome message. We planned the trial for six weeks so the team could hear how people used the guide during both quiet mornings and crowded afternoons.

The actual cost of the replacement headset was 70.21, not 153.48. The higher amount belonged to a different equipment order from the previous year and was not the price paid for these headsets. We bought twelve replacement headsets from the supplier, and the invoice lists the unit price and shipping separately. The total for this purchase was recorded in the museum equipment ledger, and the visitor services manager checked it against the receipt before the invoice was filed. The old headsets had cracked ear cups, but their cords and plugs were still usable, so the technician kept several as spare parts rather than putting them back into circulation.

We set the charging cabinet beside the information desk because staff can see its indicator lights from the entrance. The cabinet holds sixteen handsets and has a printed slot number inside each space. At closing time, the attendant checks the slots and puts any device with less than half a charge into the overnight row. The next morning, the guide lead confirms the screen brightness and plays the first track on two handsets before the doors open. This routine takes about eight minutes when every device has been returned, and longer if a visitor has taken a handset into the courtyard by mistake.

Section One: Room Sequence. The opening track explains the building was a railway office before it became a museum and points out the original iron columns near the ticket desk. Track two introduces the map gallery and asks listeners to look for the blue line painted along the floor. Track three describes the glass cases without asking visitors to touch them, and track four is a short account of the river settlement shown in the west room. The guide does not require visitors to follow the tracks in order, and the screen lets them return to the list at any time. The access note on the first page says that a printed transcript is available from the desk.

We recorded the main narration in a small meeting room upstairs with the door closed and the ventilation fan switched off. The voice artist read each passage at a steady pace and left a pause after the names of people and places so listeners could look at the relevant label. The museum educator listened to the full recording and asked us to correct the pronunciation of two family names before the files were sent to the technician. She also noticed that the east gallery track described a portrait as being on the left when it is on the right. The technician changed that direction and kept the rest of the narration unchanged.

When we tested the guide with visitors, one person said, “The room is quieter when the narration leaves a little space between the sentences.” That comment led us to check the pause lengths with the speaker held at normal listening volume. The sound was clear beside the display cases, but the first version was difficult to hear next to the large street-facing window. We moved the group listening point three steps farther into the room and added a note on the screen suggesting that visitors lower the volume before using the guide near other people. We did not add background music because the gallery already has a low, steady sound from its climate equipment.

The visitor services team also reviewed the instructions printed on the back of each handset. The original card told people to press the raised button once to begin and once again to stop the track. Staff found that some visitors expected a second press to restart the audio, so we changed the wording to explain that a second press pauses playback and the same button starts it again. The team kept the instruction short enough to fit beside the return reminder and added a small drawing of the button. The cards are wiped each evening and replaced when the corners curl or the ink begins to fade.

We keep a daily note of how many guides leave the desk and how many come back before closing. The figures are not used to identify individual visitors, and the sheet has no space for names. On the first Friday, the desk lent out thirty-eight handsets and received thirty-seven before the galleries closed. The missing device was found the next morning on a bench near the education room and had not been damaged. The attendant entered the return time in the maintenance log and placed it in the cabinet after checking its battery. That record helped the team distinguish a late return from a device that needed repair.

The audio guide is available in English during the trial, and visitors can ask the desk for a transcript if listening is not convenient. The staff have a second set of instructions for school groups because teachers sometimes collect several handsets together and return them in one batch. The group instructions ask the teacher to count the devices before leaving the desk and again at the end of the visit. No deposit is required, and the staff do not reserve handsets in advance. On busy days, the desk may ask a group to wait while returned devices are checked and charged. The trial notes will continue to include equipment costs, charging problems, and comments about particular tracks."}]
